tagline: Install Python 3, meet the REPL, run scripts, and learn print/input.

lessons.title: Installing Python 3
lessons.body:
# Installing Python 3

Everything in this course targets **Python 3** — 3.10 or newer is ideal. Python 2 died in 2020; if your machine's bare `python` command points to Python 2, ignore it and always type `python3`.

## Check what you already have

Open a terminal and run `python3 --version`. If you see something like `Python 3.12.4`, you're done — move on. If the command isn't found, install it:

- macOS: `brew install python` (or the installer from python.org)
- Windows: the installer from python.org — and check the box that says "Add python.exe to PATH"
- Linux: `sudo apt install python3` (Ubuntu/Debian) or equivalent

After installing, close and reopen your terminal, then verify with `python3 --version` again.

## One gotcha: `python` vs `python3`

On many systems, `python` still points to the ancient Python 2. Get in the habit of typing `python3` for everything in this course — running scripts, opening the REPL, installing packages. When in doubt, `python3 --version` tells you the truth.

```python
>>> import sys
>>> sys.version
'3.12.4 (main, Jun  6 2024, 18:18:56) [Clang 13.1.6 ]'
```

That snippet is also your first REPL trick: `sys.version` shows exactly which interpreter you're talking to.

```python
>>> import sys
>>> print(sys.executable)
'/usr/local/bin/python3'
```

`sys.executable` shows the exact binary being used — handy later when you juggle virtual environments and wonder which Python is actually running.
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: installing Python is like installing a JDK — but there's no compile step afterward, so the feedback loop is instant. Where you'd run `javac Main.java && java Main`, here it's just `python3 main.py`. One habit to build now: always use `python3`, never bare `python`, since bare `python` still means Python 2 on many machines (similar to how `java` vs `javac` version mismatches bite you).
keyPoints: This course targets Python 3.10+; Python 2 is dead
`sys.version` and `sys.executable` show which interpreter you're using

lessons.title: The REPL: Python's Instant Feedback Loop
lessons.body:
# The REPL: Python's Instant Feedback Loop

The REPL (read-eval-print loop) is an interactive Python session in your terminal. Type `python3` with no arguments and you get a `>>>` prompt. Whatever you type gets evaluated immediately.

```python
>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> name = "Raymond"
>>> name.upper()
'RAYMOND'
```

No compile step, no boilerplate, no `public static void main`. This is where you'll test every idea in this course before putting it in a file — think of it as a scratch pad that actually runs.

## REPL survival skills

- `exit()` or Ctrl-D quits the session.
- The up/down arrows recall previous lines (history persists between sessions on most systems).
- `_` holds the result of the last expression: type `40 + 2`, then `_ * 2`, and you get `84`.
- A `...` continuation prompt means Python is waiting for more — usually an indented block. An empty line finishes it.

```python
>>> for i in range(3):
...     print(i)
...
0
1
2
```

## When to use the REPL vs a file

Use the REPL to probe: "what does this return?", "what type is that?", "does this method exist?". Use a file for anything you want to keep. A good rule: if you typed it twice in the REPL, it belongs in a file.
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: the REPL is like JShell (`jshell` ships with the JDK) — but Python's is the default way everyone works, not an afterthought. JavaScript comparison: it's the equivalent of pasting expressions into the browser console. If you've used either, you already know the workflow; the difference is that in Python the REPL is a first-class daily tool, not a debugging sidekick.
keyPoints: `python3` with no arguments opens the REPL (`>>>` prompt)
`exit()` or Ctrl-D quits; arrow keys recall history
`_` holds the last result; `...` means "keep typing the block"
Probe ideas in the REPL; keep real code in files

lessons.title: Running .py Scripts
lessons.body:
# Running .py Scripts

Real programs live in files ending in `.py`. Create `hello.py`:

```python
name = "Raymond"
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
```

Run it from the terminal (not from inside the REPL) with `python3 hello.py`. That's the whole build-and-run cycle: edit, save, `python3 hello.py`, repeat. No compilation, no classpath, no build tool at this stage.

## Scripts vs the REPL

Anything you can type at the `>>>` prompt, you can put in a `.py` file — with one difference: the REPL automatically prints the value of every expression, but a script only prints what you explicitly `print()`. This trips up every beginner once:

```python
# in the REPL, this displays 4
>>> 2 + 2
4
```

```python
# in hello.py, this displays NOTHING
2 + 2
```

If your script runs silently, you probably computed something without printing it. Wrap it in `print()`.

## Passing arguments

Scripts read command-line arguments from `sys.argv` — a list where element 0 is the script name:

```python
import sys

print(sys.argv)
```

Run `python3 hello.py a b c` and you'll see `['hello.py', 'a', 'b', 'c']`. You'll use this pattern constantly for little utilities.
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: `python3 hello.py` replaces the whole `javac Hello.java && java Hello` dance — one step, no `.class` files littering your directory. `sys.argv` is the direct equivalent of `public static void main(String[] args)`, including the quirk that element 0 is the program name, not the first real argument.
keyPoints: Scripts are `.py` files run with `python3 file.py`
The REPL auto-prints expressions; scripts only print via `print()`
`sys.argv` holds command-line arguments (`argv[0]` is the script name)
Edit-save-run is the whole cycle — no compilation step

lessons.title: print(), input(), and Comments
lessons.body:
# print(), input(), and Comments

## print() does more than you think

`print()` takes any number of arguments and separates them with a space by default:

```python
print("The answer is", 42)
# The answer is 42
```

Two keyword arguments change its behavior: `sep` (separator between items) and `end` (what's printed after everything — a newline by default):

```python
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")
# a-b-c
print("no newline", end="")
print("same line")
# no newlinesame line
```

## input() always returns a string

`input()` pauses the program, reads one line from the keyboard, and returns it **as a string** — even if the user typed digits:

```python
name = input("Your name: ")
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
```

```python
age = input("Your age: ")
print(type(age))  # <class 'str'> -- always str!
```

Need a number? Convert it explicitly: `age = int(input("Your age: "))`. Type conversion gets its own lesson in the next module.

## Comments

A `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. There is no multi-line comment syntax — just stack `#` lines:

```python
# This whole line is a comment.
x = 5  # so is everything after the # here

# Multi-line comments are just
# several single-line comments.
```

Write comments that explain **why**, not what — `x = 5  # set x to 5` helps nobody.
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: `print()` is `System.out.println` without the ceremony, and `sep`/`end` have no direct Java equivalent — you'd build the string first. `input()` is like `new Scanner(System.in).nextLine()`: always a string, convert it yourself. JavaScript comparison: `input()` is a blocking `prompt()` that always returns a string — same stringly-typed gotcha.
keyPoints: `print()` joins arguments with spaces; `sep` and `end` customize it
`input()` always returns a string — convert with `int()`/`float()` for math
Comments start with `#`; there is no block-comment syntax
Comment the why, not the what

exercises.title: Hello, Your Name
exercises.prompt:
Write a script that stores your name in a variable called `name` and prints a greeting.

Example output:

```python
Hello, Raymond!
```

(Use any name you like.)
exercises.starterCode:
name = ""  # TODO: put your name here
# TODO: print a greeting using the name variable
hints: Build the greeting with an f-string: `f"Hello, {name}!"`
Don't forget `print()` — scripts don't auto-display values like the REPL does

exercises.title: Echo Bot
exercises.prompt:
Write a script that asks the user for their favorite programming language with `input()`, then prints it back in a sentence.

Example session:

```python
Your favorite language: Python
Python is a great choice!
```
exercises.starterCode:
# TODO: ask the user for their favorite language
# TODO: print it back in a sentence
exercises.solution:
language = input("Your favorite language: ")
print(f"{language} is a great choice!")
hints: `input("prompt")` displays the prompt and returns what the user types
The result is already a string — no conversion needed here

exercises.title: One-Line Receipt
exercises.prompt:
Using a **single** `print()` call, produce exactly this output:

```python
Item: coffee | Price: 4.50
Item: bagel  | Price: 3.25
```

Use the `sep` keyword argument — no string concatenation.
exercises.starterCode: # TODO: one print() call that produces the two-line receipt above
exercises.solution: print("Item: coffee | Price: 4.50", "Item: bagel  | Price: 3.25", sep="\n")
hints: You need a newline between the two lines — how do you write a newline inside a string?
